text: In February 1959, nine experienced ski hikers walked into the northern Urals of the Soviet Union — and never walked out.
They were students and graduates of the Ural Polytechnic in Sverdlovsk, led by a twenty-three-year-old engineer: Igor Dyatlov.
asr: They were students and graduates of the URL Polytechnic in Sverdlovsk, led by a 23-year-old engineer, Igor Dyatlov.

text: The route was demanding — a third-category winter trek. Ten set out. One turned back, sick, at the last inhabited place.
His name was Yuri Yudin. His goodbye at Vizhay became one of the most famous farewell photographs in the mountains — and the only reason this story is known.
asr: His name was Yuri Yudin. His good-bye at Vijay became one of the most famous farewell photographs in the mountains, and the only reason this story is known.

text: On the first of February, the nine climbed a saddle below a peak the local Mansi people call Kholat Syakhl — the Mountain of the Dead.
asr: On the 1st of February, the 9 climbed a saddle below a peak the local Mansi people call Collet Seaak, the mountain of the dead.

text: The last frame of their camera shows the evening camp: a step cut into the slope, and the tent pitched on it.
That night, the wind did what wind does below a ridge. It poured down the slope, hour after hour, packing snow onto the shoulder above their camp.
Sometime after half past one, the load let go. A slab of hardened snow slid onto the tent.
It did not bury them. It pressed them — hard enough to crack ribs and a skull, without leaving a single mark on the skin.
asr: It did not bury them. It pressed them hard enough to crack ribs in a skull without leaving a single mark on the skin.

text: And in the dark, they did the thing this story is remembered for: they cut their way out of their own tent — from the inside.
Outside it was minus twenty-five degrees, with wind. Some of them were in socks. Their boots stayed under the snow.
They went downhill, toward the forest line a mile and a half away. It was the right decision. In that cold, it was also a race they could not all win.
Under a giant cedar they lit a fire. Two climbed into the tree and broke branches for firewood — some five meters up.
Two died by the fire. Three turned back up the slope, toward the tent and the clothes that meant survival. None of the three reached it.
Four went lower, into a ravine by a stream, and dug a den in the snow bank. The stream kept them for three months.
The tent was found on February twenty-sixth — twenty-six days later, empty, cut open. The search went on until May.
asr: The tent was found on February 26th, 26 days later, empty, cut open. The search went on until May.

text: And the closer people looked, the stranger it seemed. Radiation on some clothing. Fatal injuries with no wounds at all. A tent cut open from the inside.
So the theories multiplied: a rocket test, ball lightning, a violent quarrel, a creature. The Soviet investigation closed after four months with one phrase: a compelling natural force.
In 2020, Russia reopened the case and concluded: an avalanche. In 2021, two Swiss engineers put the mountain into a computer — and the mountain agreed.
A step cut into the slope. Hours of wind-driven snow loading the shoulder above. A slab that waited, and then did not.
It can explain the delay, the absence of debris, even the strange injuries. It cannot be proven — no one survived to tell the story.
Today the pass carries Dyatlov's name. Nine cut, as it were, from one sheet — and the tenth man carried their story for the rest of his life.
asr: Today, the past carries Diet Love's name, nine cut, as it were, from one sheet, and the tenth man carried their story for the rest of his life.

text: Some mountains keep their dead. This one kept their question.
